points.title: La grammaire du français familier : ce qui change structurellement, pas seulement le vocabulaire
points.explanationEn:
Familiar/spoken French is not simply standard French with slang words swapped in — it runs on a systematically different, internally consistent GRAMMAR that every native speaker uses in casual contexts and that C1 learners must recognize and be able to produce, because sounding exclusively 'textbook-correct' in casual conversation reads as stiff, foreign, or oddly formal to native ears. The four structural shifts below are not sloppiness; they are the actual rules of spoken register, learned natively before children ever encounter the written standard.

First, ne-drop in negation: standard written French requires both ne and pas (je ne sais pas), but spoken familier French overwhelmingly drops the ne and keeps only pas (or another negative word): je sais pas, j'ai pas compris, y a pas de problème. This isn't an error native speakers make — it's the default spoken form, to the point that including a carefully pronounced ne in casual conversation can sound performed or overly careful. The negative word (pas, rien, jamais, plus, personne) still does the actual work of negating; ne was already semantically empty in modern French and its loss in speech simply completes a change that's been underway for over a century. Written informal registers (texting, casual emails between friends) mirror this: 'jsp' (je sais pas), 'chuis pas sûr' (je suis pas sûr) both drop the ne in writing too.

Second, on systematically replaces nous as the subject pronoun for 'we' in spoken French, while nous survives mainly as a stressed/disjunctive pronoun (avec nous, nous, on y va) or in writing. Crucially, on takes third-person-singular verb agreement even though it means 'we': on va au cinéma (we're going to the movies), not the standard-register nous allons au cinéma — and when a following adjective agrees with the real, understood plural subject, you can get the hybrid on est fatigués (we are tired) with a plural agreement on a grammatically singular verb, which looks 'wrong' by the rules of formal grammar but is completely standard spoken usage.

Third, question formation in casual speech drops inversion (which sounds formal/written: viens-tu?) almost entirely, replacing it with either simple rising intonation on a statement-order sentence (tu viens ?) or, for information questions, keeping the question word at the end or start without inverting the subject and verb: t'as vu qui ? (instead of qui as-tu vu ?) or c'est où, ça ? (instead of où est-ce ?). Est-ce que remains available and common across registers as a middle ground, but pure inversion is now essentially confined to written French and highly formal/careful spoken French.

Fourth, the tu/vous register switch operates on different social rules in familier contexts than the textbook 'strangers get vous, friends get tu' simplification suggests. Among peers under a certain age gap, in casual professional settings in many industries (tech, media, creative fields), and always among students, tu has become the unmarked default, and offering vous can even read as distancing or sarcastic. Conversely, switching from vous to tu (tutoiement) is itself a grammatical/social event — French has a verb for it, tutoyer (on peut se tutoyer ? — 'can we use tu with each other?') — and getting the timing wrong (tutoying too early signals presumption; staying on vous too long signals coldness) is a fluency marker in itself, not just a vocabulary issue.

examples.fr: Je sais pas si je vais venir ce soir, j'suis crevé.
examples.en: I don't know if I'm coming tonight, I'm exhausted.
examples.note: ne dropped from je (ne) sais pas; j'suis is the casual elision of je suis

examples.fr: On se voit demain ? On a plein de trucs à se dire.
examples.en: Shall we see each other tomorrow? We have loads of things to talk about.
examples.note: on replacing nous as subject, singular verb form (a) despite plural meaning

examples.fr: T'as pas vu mes clés, par hasard ?
examples.en: You haven't seen my keys, by any chance?
examples.note: t'as = tu as, elided; pas alone carries the negation, no ne
on + singular verb (est) but plural adjective agreement (fatigués) — a hybrid unique to spoken on-for-nous

examples.fr: T'as vu qui à la soirée hier ?
examples.en: Who did you see at the party yesterday?
examples.note: no inversion; question word stays where a statement would put the answer, matching spoken rhythm

examples.fr: C'est à quelle heure, le film ?
examples.note: topic-first ordering with c'est, avoiding both inversion and est-ce que

examples.fr: Y a plus de café, faut en racheter.
examples.en: There's no more coffee, we need to buy more.
examples.note: y a = il y a (il dropped entirely in fast speech); faut = il faut, same pattern

examples.fr: On peut se tutoyer, si tu veux, on n'est pas obligés de rester sur le vous.
examples.en: We can use tu with each other, if you want — we don't have to stick with vous.
examples.note: se tutoyer is the reflexive verb for 'to use tu'; note this sentence itself keeps a careful ne, showing register can mix in transitional social moments

examples.fr: Chuis pas sûr que ce soit une bonne idée, franchement.
examples.en: I'm not sure that's a good idea, honestly.
examples.note: chuis = je suis, heavily elided in fast/written-casual French (texting register)

examples.fr: Vous pouvez me tutoyer, hein, on n'est pas à un enterrement.
examples.en: You can use tu with me, you know, we're not at a funeral.
examples.note: explicit invitation to switch registers — the offer itself is made in vous, a common transitional pattern

commonMistakes: Keeping a carefully pronounced ne in casual conversation with friends, which is not wrong but sounds noticeably stiff and overly careful compared to the natural je sais pas / j'ai pas.
Using nous + plural verb in casual spoken contexts (nous allons au cinéma) where every native speaker would say on va au cinéma, making the learner sound like they're reading from a textbook.

Forgetting that on still triggers singular verb agreement even when a following adjective is plural, producing errors like on sont fatigués (verb wrongly pluralized) instead of the correct on est fatigués.
Overusing full subject-verb inversion (viens-tu ? as-tu vu ?) in casual speech, which is grammatically perfect but registers as unnaturally formal or literary among peers.

Misjudging the tu/vous switch — staying on vous too long with same-age peers (reads as cold/distant) or tutoying an elder/superior too early (reads as presumptuous), because textbook rules ('strangers = vous') don't capture the more fluid social calculus of real usage.
whyItTrips: Textbooks teach standard written French almost exclusively, so learners arrive at C1 having drilled ne...pas, nous, and inversion as 'the rules,' with no exposure to the fact that native speakers systematically deviate from those same rules in every casual conversation.

English has no grammaticalized T-V distinction (tu/vous) at all, so English speakers have no native instinct for reading social register off of pronoun choice, and no felt sense that switching pronouns mid-relationship is itself a meaningful, sometimes delicate act.

Because these familier patterns are consistent and rule-governed rather than random 'errors,' they're easy to mistake for sloppiness to be avoided, when in fact producing zero familier grammar in casual settings is itself the marked, unnatural choice.
